endorsements.quote: Where assessments cannot yet be conducted directly, document compensating controls (e.g., obtaining vendor SOC 2 reports, requiring third-party pen test summaries).

endorsements.quote: U sers should be provided education on AI cybersecurity fundamentals, including specific cybersecurity risks that AI systems can face, evolving tactics of AI cyber attackers, and the user’s role in mitigating threats and reporting suspicious AI behavior or outputs.

endorsements.quote: For this step, the team should determine whether there is a training curriculum and related materials for the AI solution, and if so, whether it provides for training for specialized roles.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence in Dental Education: Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models and Multimodal Foundation Models
endorsements.quote: Train students and staff on handling personal health information through scenario-based exercises, ensuring they understand how to manage data securely when using LLM or FM in dental settings.

endorsements.title: Quo Vadis, AI-Empowered Doctor?
endorsements.quote: Physicians should understand how privacy and confidentiality may be breached by incautious use of public LLM models.

endorsements.title: Strengthening Ethical Practices of Patient Data Confidentiality and Sharing Among Nurses in the Artificial Intelligence-Driven Healthcare Era
endorsements.quote: Studies mentioned that nurses have many responsibilities that include offering regular training focused on legal frameworks (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), securing data handling, and integrating AI in clinical systems for all employees who participated in patient care.

evidence.title: Medical students' use of large language models: a national survey
evidence.outcome: Self-reported adequacy of education on data privacy regulations for LLM tools
evidence.effect: Only 21.43% of respondents felt adequately educated on data privacy regulations applicable to these tools.
evidence.quote: Only 21.43% of respondents felt adequately educated on data privacy regulations applicable to these tools.

commentary.bottom_line: Six sources endorse training staff on AI privacy and security threats, but no study has tested whether such training reduces shadow AI use, data exposure, or attacks. One survey of 286 Canadian medical students found that 21.43% felt adequately educated on privacy regulations for LLM tools, which documents a knowledge gap rather than a remedy.

perspectives.view: No study in this map tests whether AI privacy and security training changes staff behavior, data exposure, or attack rates. The one related study is a cross-sectional survey of 286 medical students, of whom 21.43% felt adequately educated on privacy rules for LLM tools. It shows that a gap exists but does not measure the effect of training.

The survey suggests that many trainees may use LLM tools without feeling prepared to protect patient data, which is a plausible route to disclosure. No study reports suspicious-activity reporting rates, privacy incidents, or near misses before and after training. It is therefore unknown whether training stops unsafe use before patient information leaves the organization.

The survey sampled medical students, not the staff, IT personnel, privileged users, or executives that the recommendation names. No study describes curriculum content, training time, refresher frequency, or completion rates. The workflow burden and fidelity of role-specific AI security training in a working health system have not been measured.

The only study surveyed medical students in Canada and did not examine patients or care settings. No evidence addresses whether untrained or shadow AI use exposes data from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients at different rates. It also does not show whether training protects these patients.

commentary.research_gap: Controlled before-and-after studies or cluster trials are needed that deliver role-specific AI privacy and security training to clinical staff, IT personnel, privileged users, and executives. These studies should measure unsanctioned AI tool use, reporting of suspicious AI behavior, simulated attack outcomes, and actual data exposure events.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the single hazard study surveyed Canadian medical students without reference to Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether training reduces data exposure risk for their patients.
